title: Review of the effects of plants on indoor environments
review_question: What are the effects of plants on indoor air quality and the broader benefits of incorporating vegetation into indoor environments?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly stated; the review adopts a narrative approach, synthesizing findings from various studies on indoor plants and nature exposure.

synthesis_conclusions: Indoor plants have a demonstrated capacity to improve indoor air quality by removing various toxins (e.g., formaldehyde, VOCs, CO2, ammonia, particulate matter).
Plants in indoor environments offer significant psychological benefits, including improved mental well-being, positive mood, prosocial behavior, and reduced anxiety and tension.
Physiological benefits of indoor plants include improved overall health, reduced illness, stress reduction, decreased sick leave, and potentially lowered mortality.
Cognitive benefits include attention restoration, reduced ADD/ADHD symptoms, reduced mental fatigue, and improvements in productivity and attitude.
The integration of plant-based systems into buildings offers a more affordable and ecologically sound means of improving IAQ compared to mechanical systems.

Building-integrated plant systems, while promising for whole-building air filtration, have disadvantages related to size, inflexibility, embodied energy, and maintenance (e.g., water consumption, mould risk).
evidence_gaps: Research is largely limited to sealed and controlled chambers, making extrapolation to real-world settings challenging.
More field testing is needed, particularly on the capacity of plants to reduce energy consumption in room-scale applications.
A need for more objective measurements to reduce reliance on self-reported data and potential response bias (demand characteristics, social desirability).
The effectiveness of plants in remediating radon, asbestos, lead, and certain hydrocarbons (e.g., propane, butane, methyl chloroform, methylene chloride) has yet to be investigated.
The direct relationship between the phytoremediation capacity of plants and improved physiological states remains unclear.
Further research is needed on the effects of indoor plants on allergies and lung disease (including asthma).
More systematic research is needed on the effect of indoor plants on various age groups, controlling for factors like activity choices.
A deeper understanding of the nature of human-plant interaction (e.g., passive vs. active, direct vs. indirect exposure) is required.
It is difficult to create controlled outdoor environments for comparison, limiting research on indoor vs. outdoor settings.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Not explicitly performed as a systematic assessment; however, the paper acknowledges limitations related to self-reported data and the generalizability of findings from controlled settings.
heterogeneity_sources: Differences in plant species and growing media affect toxin removal capacity.
Variations in plant density and placement in relation to workstations influence productivity effects.
The type of work performed (creative vs. mundane) can moderate the impact on performance.
Demographic variations (gender, age) can influence psychological and physiological responses to plants.
The nature of interaction with nature (passive vs. active, direct vs. indirect) may influence psychological effects.

moderators.effect: Flowering plants had a more positive effect on women, while general vegetation displays had a more positive effect on men. Women report negative side effects of SBS more often than men, especially with fewer plants.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Women show more positive response to flowering plants; men to general vegetation. Women report higher SBS symptoms with fewer plants.

moderators.effect: Plants have a positive effect on creative tasks but may negatively affect mundane or routine tasks initially, though performance on routine tasks may improve over time due to restorative effects.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Positive for creative tasks; mixed/initially negative for mundane tasks, improving over time.

moderators.effect: Hydroponic systems with carbon filters and exposed root zones are significantly more effective at pollutant removal than plants potted in standard soil. Plant species vary in their toxin removal capacity.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Hydroponic systems are more effective; specific plant species target different toxins.

limitations: Many findings apply to nature broadly rather than specifically to indoor vegetation, making them suggestive rather than conclusive for indoor settings.
The majority of information is self-reported, leading to potential response bias (demand characteristics, social desirability).
Research is often conducted in sealed and controlled chambers with high plant density, making it difficult to extrapolate to real-world conditions.

Building-integrated plant systems have disadvantages such as large size, inflexibility, significant embodied energy, and potential for mould/bacteria growth due to uncontrolled plant growth and water consumption.
The direct relationship between the phytoremediation capacity of plants and improved physiological states is still unclear.
There is a need for more systematic research on the effects of indoor plants across different age groups and genders.
It is challenging to create controlled outdoor environments for direct comparison with indoor settings.

paper_metadata.title: Review of the effects of plants on indoor environments
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Review of the effects of plants on indoor environments
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Although well-established technologies can remove certain toxins from indoor environments, methods capable of eliminating all of them do not yet exist. Biological methods, however, which are based on plants and their associated microorganisms, could hold significant promise. To achieve high toxic remediation, utilization of the soil microorganisms in the root zone of the plant is vital. Moreover, evidence suggests that in addition to cleaning the air, plants in indoor environments offer psychological, physiological and cognitive benefits. This paper provides an overview of the effects of plants on indoor air quality on the broader benefits of incorporating vegetation into indoor environments.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural elements like indoor plants can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue, consistent with ART principles.
Humans have an innate tendency to connect with nature, and indoor plants satisfy this need, leading to psychological and physiological benefits.
Viewing natural scenes or elements like plants can elicit positive emotional states and reduce physiological stress.

mechanism_chain.description: The review synthesizes multiple proposed mechanisms linking indoor plants to human well-being and performance, encompassing psychological, physiological, and environmental pathways.

instruments_used.name: PANAS (Positive and Negative Affect Schedule)
instruments_used.description: A common self-report measure for assessing current mood states.

instruments_used.name: Profile of Mood States (POMS)
instruments_used.construct: mood states (e.g., tension, depression, anger, vigor, fatigue, confusion)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire used to assess transient mood states.

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.construct: physiological stress response / autonomic nervous system activity
instruments_used.description: A physiological measure derived from electrocardiogram (ECG) data, indicating stress or relaxation.

instruments_used.name: Cognitive performance tests
instruments_used.description: Various behavioral tasks such as proofreading, digit span, or reaction time tests used to assess cognitive function.

instruments_used.name: Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire designed to measure the perceived restorative qualities of an environment, based on Attention Restoration Theory.
